Aldabra cassia
Chamaecrista aldabrensis
Cassia aldabrensis

A low, spreading perennial subshrub of the Aldabra islands, with slender stems woody at the base and fine puberulence. Its short leaves carry 3–9 pairs of minute, oblong leaflets, each asymmetric about its midrib; a small sessile gland may occur near the basal pair. The extra-axillary inflorescence usually bears one small yellow flower. Hairy pods are about 2–2.5 cm long. The tree index uses the older name Cassia aldabrensis; Kew accepts Chamaecrista aldabrensis.
Recorded on Aldabra and Assumption in the Seychelles; the specialist Seychelles flora describes it as presumed endemic to Aldabra, while a recent flora also records it on Assumption.
A 15–40 cm, low, spreading perennial subshrub; older stems become woody at the base.
Leaves only 1–1.5 cm long, with 3–9 pairs of oblong leaflets about 3 × 0.8 mm; the leaflets are asymmetric and the rachis often has a sessile gland beside the basal pair.
Usually one extra-axillary flower; its five unequal petals are yellow and about 5–6 mm long.
A puberulent, dehiscent pod about 2–2.5 cm long; the small seeds bear aligned dark markings.
The checked flora gives no transferable flowering or fruiting calendar.
Archbold’s aglaia
Aglaia archboldiana
Aglaia archboldiana

A slender forest tree of Viti Levu, Fiji, recorded from near sea level to about 970 m and reaching roughly 10 m. A.C. Smith described a light-brown indument on young parts and exceptionally large compound leaves, which help distinguish it from its closest relative, A. parksii. The original author later corrected his description of the petals: the outer petals have sparse hairs near their base. The consulted species account does not establish mature fruit characters or flower colour.
Known from Viti Levu, Fiji; collections are from dense forest over a broad elevational range.
A slender forest tree, reported up to about 10 m, with light-brown hairs on young growth.
Very large pinnate leaves; the species account emphasizes their size, while detailed leaflet measurements are not supplied here.
The outer petals bear sparse hairs toward their bases. The checked species description does not confirm corolla colour; the pale tone in the plate is illustrative.
Mature fruit characters were not established in the sources consulted, so no diagnostic fruit appearance is claimed.
The consulted type-based account does not provide a reliable flowering or fruiting calendar.
Taveuni brown-leaf syzygium
Syzygium phaeophyllum
Eugenia durifolia; Syzygium durifolium (illegitimate later homonym)

A very poorly known evergreen tree endemic to Taveuni, Fiji, represented by early twentieth-century collections from dense forest near Somosomo. The recorded tree reached about 6 m and had smooth bark and stiff, cylindrical brown twigs. Its leathery elliptic leaves measure about 6–8 × 2.5–4 cm, taper slightly at the base and end in an acuminate tip; the flattened petiole is 6–10 mm long. Flower and fruit details are not secure in the sources consulted. Kew accepts the 1945 name Syzygium phaeophyllum; a later homonymous combination is not the accepted name.
Known from Taveuni, Fiji, in wet tropical forest; the type was collected at roughly 700–900 m east of Somosomo.
An evergreen tree recorded to about 6 m, with smooth bark and stiff, round brown twigs.
Leathery elliptic blades about 6–8 × 2.5–4 cm; base slightly narrowed, apex acuminate, petiole flattened and 6–10 mm long.
Species-specific flower form and colour are not confirmed by the checked records; the plate therefore uses foliage only.
Species-specific fruit form and colour are not confirmed by the checked records.
The available collections do not support a reliable annual phenology calendar.
Lake Atitlán coral tree
Erythrina atitlanensis
Erythrina atitlanensis

A deciduous Guatemalan tree described from flowering material collected above San Juan La Laguna, Lake Atitlán, at about 1,585 m. Like other Erythrina, it bears alternate, three-foliolate leaves and showy papilionoid flowers; the genus has prickles on some petioles or branches and usually red-to-orange corollas. Species-level field data remain sparse, so the exact wild stature, detailed leaflet measurements and fruit characters should be treated cautiously. The red flower shown agrees with documented cultivated flowering but is not a measurement from the type.
Known from Guatemala around Lake Atitlán; the cited isotype records flowering in February at about 1,585 m.
A deciduous tree; cultivated references report roughly 6–12 m, but the consulted type record does not give a measured height.
Alternate leaves divided into three leaflets; the terminal leaflet is commonly the largest in the genus. Petioles and young branches can bear prickles.
Showy red papilionoid flowers in an upright raceme, consistent with cultivated records and the usual floral form of Erythrina.
As a legume, it produces a pod; species-specific pod shape, size and seed details were not confirmed in the sources consulted.
The isotype is flowering in February; this single collection does not establish the full seasonal calendar.
Bahia pink cactus
Pierrebraunia bahiensis
Arrojadoa bahiensis; Floribunda bahiensis

A compact succulent subshrub endemic to Bahia, Brazil, on rocky, seasonally dry ground. Young shoots are nearly spherical; mature stems are short cylindrical to columnar, often branching at or below the base, commonly around 30 cm but occasionally much taller. The green to grey-green stems carry 9–14(–17) rounded ribs, initially woolly areoles, one central spine and several radial spines. Pink narrow tubular flowers open at night; pink naked berries contain black seeds. POWO accepts Pierrebraunia bahiensis, while some cactus classifications have treated it as Arrojadoa.
Endemic to Bahia, northeastern Brazil, especially rocky quartzitic and sandstone sites in the Chapada Diamantina.
A low succulent subshrub, usually around 30 cm tall; older plants may branch at the base and occasionally exceed 60 cm.
True leaves are reduced; the visible armature is made of woolly areoles on 9–14 rounded ribs, each bearing a central spine and several radial spines.
Narrow tubular pink flowers, about 3.2–3.9 cm long, arise near the upper stem and open at night; inner perianth parts are white.
A naked pink berry, roughly 1–3 cm across, with white pulp and small black seeds.
No reliable wild flowering or fruiting calendar was found in the checked specialist sources.
Ríos-Saña cactus
Rauhocereus riosaniensis
Browningia riosaniensis

A large branching columnar cactus of northern Peru, usually branching from the base and forming dense stands. Its bluish-green shoots are roughly 8–15 cm thick; 5–6 longitudinal ribs are divided by transverse grooves into flattened tubercles. Woolly areoles carry a few strong spines, sometimes up to about 5 cm. Large funnel-shaped white flowers open at night; their scaly tube bears curly brown hairs. The fleshy ovoid fruit is dark red, with a persistent flower remnant and shiny black seeds.
Northern Peru, including the Saña, Chamaya and Jaén valleys; dry scrub and river-valley settings.
A shrubby columnar cactus branching from a thick trunk or from the base; plants may reach about 4 m.
Leaves are absent; the diagnostic surface has 5–6 wavy ribs broken into flattened tubercles, with woolly areoles and 2–8 robust spines.
Large white bell-to-funnel flowers, about 8–10 cm long, open at night; brown curled hairs sit in the axils of the scales on the flower tube.
A red fleshy ovoid berry with a persistent dry flower remnant and small shiny black seeds.
Flowers open at night; the consulted flora does not establish a reliable month-by-month calendar.
